parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem:
Coherent visible light of a single frequency is incident normally on a double slit. This produces a pattern of bright and dark interference fringes on a screen, as illustrated in Fig. 6.1.
{{figure:figure_6_1}}
Fig. 6.1 (not to scale)
There are seven bright fringes.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Explain how the pattern of bright and dark interference fringes is formed.

markscheme_points.text: Any three from: • Light diffracts at the (two) slits. • Light (from each slit) meets / superposes (at the screen). • When the phase difference is 0 (degrees) a bright fringe / (intensity) maximum is formed. • When the phase difference is 180 (degrees) a dark fringe / (intensity) minimum is formed.

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking what happens to the light as it passes through each narrow slit and spreads out toward the screen.
Hint 2: Now think about what happens where the two spreading waves meet on the screen - how do their displacements combine?
Hint 3: Link bright and dark to how in-step the two waves arrive - what phase difference gives reinforcement and what gives cancellation?
parts.proper_answer: Light diffracts at the two slits and the waves from each slit superpose at the screen. Where phase difference is $0$ constructive interference gives a bright fringe (maximum). Where phase difference is $180^{\circ}$ destructive interference gives a dark fringe (minimum).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spreading From Each Slit**
You have coherent light of one frequency falling on two very narrow slits. Each slit acts as a new source and the light diffracts, so it spreads out. That means light from the top slit and light from the bottom slit can both reach the same point on the screen.

Step 2: **Meeting and Adding**
At any point on the screen the displacement is the sum of the displacements from the two waves. This is superposition. Because the light is coherent, the phase relationship between the two waves is fixed, so a stable interference pattern forms.

Step 3: **Bright Versus Dark**
If the two waves arrive in step, crest on crest, the path difference gives a phase difference of $0$. They reinforce and you get constructive interference, a bright fringe with maximum intensity. If they arrive in antiphase, crest on trough, the phase difference is $180^{\circ}$. They cancel and you get destructive interference, a dark fringe with minimum intensity.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
The distance between the centres of bright fringe $X$ and bright fringe $Y$ in the pattern is $10.2\text{ mm}$. The slit spacing is $1.2\text{ mm}$. The distance from the slits to the screen is $3.1\text{ m}$.
Calculate the wavelength of the light incident on the slits.
hints: Hint 1: The 10.2 mm is not one fringe width - count how many gaps there are between 7 bright fringes from X to Y to get one fringe separation $x$.
Hint 2: Check all lengths are in metres before you calculate - convert slit spacing $a$ and fringe width $x$ from mm to m, $D$ is already in m.
Hint 3: Combine $a$, $x$ and $D$ with the two-slit interference relationship to find $\lambda$ and give it to 2 significant figures in m.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find One Fringe Width**
A common slip is to use 10.2 mm as $x$. Look at Fig. 6.1: X to Y spans 7 bright fringes, so there are 6 intervals between them. So one fringe separation is $$x = \frac{10.2 \times 10^{-3}}{6} = 1.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **List Values in SI Units**
Slit separation $a = 1.2\text{ mm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Screen distance $D = 3.1\text{ m}$. Fringe width $x = 1.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ as above.

Step 3: **Apply Two-Slit Equation**
For a double slit, fringe separation and wavelength are linked by $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ Rearranged: $$\lambda = \frac{ax}{D}$$ Put the numbers in: $$\lambda = \frac{(1.2 \times 10^{-3})(1.7 \times 10^{-3})}{3.1} = 6.6 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$$ This is red light, sensible for visible light.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
The light is replaced by different visible light with a shorter wavelength.
State how the new fringe separation will compare to the original fringe separation.
hints: Hint 1: Recall how fringe separation $x$ depends on wavelength $\lambda$ when $a$ and $D$ are unchanged.
parts.proper_answer: New fringe separation is smaller (fringes closer together).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Proportionality**
Since $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ with $a$ and $D$ fixed, $x$ is directly proportional to $\lambda$. A shorter $\lambda$ gives a smaller $x$, so the whole pattern squeezes together.

enrichment.label: (a)(iii)
key_concepts: proportionality of fringe separation to wavelength

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A stationary wave is formed on a stretched string $AB$, as shown in Fig. 6.2.
{{figure:figure_6_2}}
Fig. 6.2
$P$, $Q$ and $R$ are points on the string.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 6.2, draw a cross ($\times$) to show the position of a node.

markscheme_points.text: A cross at the intersection of the string and the mean position line.

hints: Hint 1: Think where on a stationary wave the string never moves from its mean position - where does the string cross the dashed mean line?
parts.proper_answer: Mark a cross ($\times$) at any point where the string crosses the dashed mean position line, e.g. between A and the first trough, or between the loops. This is a node of zero vibration.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Node**
A node is a point of always zero displacement. On the diagram the string moves up and down, but where it crosses the dashed mean position line it stays at zero. Any one of those crossing points is a node. Put your $\times$ exactly on the intersection of the solid string and the dashed line.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the phase difference between $P$ and $Q$.
hints: Hint 1: Check whether P and Q are in the same vibrating loop between two adjacent nodes and moving in the same direction together.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Same Loop Means In Step**
P and Q are both on the same central hump, between the same two nodes. In a stationary wave all points between adjacent nodes vibrate in phase, reaching maximum and zero together. So the phase difference is $0^{\circ}$.

enrichment.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: in-phase points in same loop of stationary wave

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: State the phase difference between $P$ and $R$.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the loop containing P with the loop containing R - what happens to one loop when the adjacent loop moves up?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Adjacent Loops Are Opposite**
P is on the upper middle loop and R is on the lower right loop. Adjacent loops in a stationary wave always move in opposite directions - when one goes up the other goes down. They are in antiphase, so the phase difference is $180^{\circ}$.
